summary.text: An asymptote of a curve is a straight line that the curve approaches, in the sense that the distance between them goes to zero as x or y tends to infinity.
There are three kinds of asymptotes: horizontal, vertical and oblique.
Asymptotes show how a curve behaves in the large, and finding them is an important step in sketching a function's graph.

facts.label: Introduced by
facts.value: Apollonius of Perga, in his work on conic sections

facts.label: Rational function case
facts.value: Vertical asymptote where the denominator is zero and the numerator is not

facts.label: Graph of 1/x
facts.value: Both axes are asymptotes of its curve

items.prompt: On a screen, a line and a curve seem to merge far out, yet mathematicians say they only approach each other. Why?

options.label: Real curves eventually bend away from lines
Screens round values, so the picture is simply too coarse
Marks on a screen have width, but ideal lines and curves have width 0
The merging is an optical effect of drawing it on paper

items.explain: Marks on paper or pixels have positive width, but the line and the curve are idealized concepts whose width is 0. So grasping an asymptote takes reason rather than experience.

items.prompt: On the curve of 1/x, x grows through 100, 1,000, 10,000 and the height shrinks toward the axis. Does the curve ever land on the x-axis?

options.label: Yes, once x is huge enough, the height rounds to 0
Yes, but only at infinity itself
No, 1/x is never 0, however large x becomes
No, but only because the curve is drawn too thin to reach

items.explain: No matter how large x becomes, its reciprocal 1/x is never 0, so the curve never actually touches the x-axis.

items.prompt: A rational function has a denominator equal to zero at some input, while the numerator does not. What does its graph show there?

options.label: A vertical asymptote
A horizontal asymptote
An oblique asymptote
A point where the graph meets the axis

items.explain: A common example of a vertical asymptote is a rational function at a point where the denominator is zero and the numerator is non-zero.

items.prompt: A function's graph is drawn with a vertical asymptote. At most how many times can the graph meet that asymptote?

options.label: At most once
Twice, once from each side
Any number of times, if the curve wiggles
Exactly once for every function

items.explain: It is impossible for the graph of a function to intersect a vertical line in more than one point.

items.prompt: As x grows very large, a graph keeps getting closer to a slanted line whose slope is not zero. What kind of asymptote is that line?

options.label: Horizontal
Vertical
Curvilinear
Oblique

items.explain: An oblique asymptote has a slope that is non-zero but finite, and the graph approaches it as x tends to +∞ or −∞.

items.prompt: A graph levels off at one height far to the right and at a different height far to the left. How many horizontal asymptotes does it have?

options.label: One, since a graph has a single end behaviour
Two, one for each end
None, since it levels off at two heights
As many as there are heights it passes through

items.explain: The arctangent has y = π/2 as a horizontal asymptote as x tends to +∞ and y = –π/2 as x tends to –∞.
